prompt: Why does a lower bound for comparisons averaged over every distinct-key permutation still allow linear-time sorting on an already sorted array?

options.text: A favourable input is only one case
options.explanation: Correct: the average combines all equally likely permutations, rather than imposing that cost on each one.
It applies to every correct comparison sort, including algorithms with logarithmic factors.

options.text: Already sorted values are not distinct
options.explanation: Distinct keys can be already sorted; distinctness does not prevent an adaptive fast path.

options.text: Random pivots eliminate the average bound
options.explanation: Randomness does not remove the information needed to distinguish the uniformly distributed permutations.

workedExample: An adaptive sort can recognise an ordered run with one sequential pass. It still has to distinguish every other ordering on less favourable inputs. The comparison lower bound constrains the average over the whole uniform input distribution, not the cost of the single sorted ordering.
